name: Scottish Gaelic
notes: Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig). ~57,000 speakers (2011 census). Highlands and Islands of Scotland. PERVASIVE BROAD/SLENDER (leathann/caol) CONSONANT QUALITY: a consonant is slender (palatalised) beside ⟨e i⟩ and broad beside ⟨a o u⟩ ('caol le caol agus leathann le leathann'), and the flanking vowel letter that signals the quality is very often NOT itself pronounced — it is a quality marker, not a nucleus. Both halves are encoded in positional_graphemes: consonants take before_front_vowel/after_front_vowel slender variants, and the marker vowels map to the empty string. Stops are voiceless throughout (⟨b d g⟩ = unaspirated /p t̪ k/, ⟨p t c⟩ = aspirated), and slender velars are palatalised /kʲ kʲʰ/ rather than palatal /c ɟ/. Preaspiration of ⟨p t c⟩ after stressed vowels is encoded (GD_PREASP_*): [hp ht hk] broadly, with the velar realised as [x] before broad ⟨c⟩ (mac [maxk]). The realisation is strongly dialectal — six distinct patterns are attested — so the rules encode the central/general pattern only, matching the Lewis-dialect data in Oftedal (1956) and in Nance & Ó Maolalaigh (2020) (whose informant is from Ness, Isle of Lewis), not the dialect variation generally. Svarabhakti — an unwritten epenthetic vowel breaking up a sonorant+consonant cluster (arm [aɾam], ainm [anam], balg [palʲak], Alba [alʲapə]; Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2020) — is real but is NOT encoded here: unlike Irish, where the epenthetic vowel reduces to a fixed /ə/ (modelled in the ga spec's GA_SVARABHAKTI_* rules), the Gaelic epenthetic vowel usually COPIES the preceding vowel's quality, which this engine's phoneme-triggered rewrite rules cannot express without enumerating a rule per vowel×sonorant×cluster combination; deferred rather than shipped half-modelled. Measured against the wikipron gold (n=3719): folding preaspiration out of both sides moves PER from 0.3202 to 0.3205, and folding a crude svarabhakti approximation moves it to 0.3264 (worse) — neither phenomenon is the dominant error source; the gold itself mixes at least two notational traditions for ⟨b d g⟩ (185/3720 words carry the Borgstrøm/Oftedal-style devoicing diacritic d̥/ɡ̊/b̥ that this spec does not use, following Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2020's aspiration-based analysis) and mixes dialects (986/3720 words carry 2+ mutually incompatible pronunciations). Refs: Nance & Ó Maolalaigh (2020), Bauer (2011), Ó Maolalaigh (2008). Inventory and preaspiration cross-checked against Gillies (2009) and Ó Baoill (2010).

sources.notes: Fetched and read directly (open-access PDF via the author's site). Speaker recorded is from Ness, Isle of Lewis. Source for the consonant inventory (/pʰ p tʰ̪ t̪ tʲʰ tʲ kʰ k/ etc.), the word-initial-stress generalisation, and the dialectal variation in preaspiration realisation (voiceless [h] in Lewis, more [x]-like in Barra per Ó Murchú 1985, longest in velar/palatal stops and shortest in bilabials). Also states explicitly that orthographic ⟨b d g⟩ show 'very little or no closure voicing even in word-medial stops' (citing Nance & Stuart-Smith 2013), so the contrast is aspiration (/pʰ/ vs /p/) rather than voicing — the analysis this spec follows. Describes svarabhakti (unwritten epenthetic vowel breaking up a sonorant+consonant cluster, usually copying the preceding vowel, e.g. arm [aɾam], ainm [anam], balg [palʲak], Alba [alʲapə]) as real but NOT encoded in this spec (see notes).

location.notes: Glottolog's representative point for Scottish Gaelic.

allophone_rules.notes: Preaspiration: Scottish Gaelic preaspirates the aspirated stops ⟨p t c⟩ medially and finally after a stressed vowel — the diagnostic feature that separates Gaelic from Irish (Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2020; Ó Maolalaigh 2008). The realisation is strongly dialectal (six attested patterns, [xk ht hp] ~ [ʰk ʰt ʰp] ~ none); the mainstream pattern encoded here is [xk]/[çkʲ] for the velars and [h]+stop for the coronals and labials. Conditioned on a preceding vowel, so word-initial and post-consonantal stops keep their plain aspirated realisation.

stress.notes: Scottish Gaelic stresses the FIRST syllable of the word (Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2020); unstressed vowels reduce to /ə/.
